# Frequentist Hypothesis Testing {#sec-freq-hypothesis-test}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

```{ojs}
bodyFont = getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily
```

:::

Recalling the <span class="xref-no-num">[main inference tasks @sec-inference-tasks]</span>, we now move from *interval estimation* to *hypothesis testing*.

The name **hypothesis testing** comes from the **scientific method**:

1. Propose a hypothesis about the world.
2. Collect data through experiment or observation.
3. Assess whether the data are consistent with the hypothesis.

If the data are consistent, this provides **support** for the hypothesis (though never proof). If the data look very unlikely under the hypothesis, this is evidence *against* it.

Unlike **interval estimation** (which gives a range of plausible values), hypothesis testing asks a **yes/no question** about the parameter $\theta$.

To make this precise, we specify a **null hypothesis** $H_0$, a concrete mathematical statement about $\theta$:
$$
H_0 : \theta \in \Theta_0,
$$

where $\Theta_0 \subseteq \Theta$ is part of the parameter space.

The **alternative hypothesis** is simply the complement set:
$$
H_1 : \theta \in \Theta \setminus \Theta_0,
$$
i.e. the parameter values in $\Theta$ which are not in $\Theta_0$.

So every hypothesis test is really just a <span class="xref-no-num">[partition @def-excl-exh-part]</span> of the parameter space into two regions: one where the null holds, and one where it does not.


::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### One-Dimensional Parameter Space
```{ojs}
//| label: fig-theta-partition
//| fig-cap: Partition of the parameter space $\Theta$ into $\Theta_0$ (null) and $H_1=\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$. Example shown is a one-sided null $H_0\colon\,\mu \le \mu_0$.

thetaPartition = {
  const width = 540, height = 120, pad = 28;

  // Axis and μ0 location (tweak the 0.58 to move μ0)
  const mu0x = width * 0.58;

  // Colors (CSS variables with sensible fallbacks)
  const colH0   = "var(--brand-teal, #14b8a6)";
  const colH1   = "var(--brand-red,  #ef4444)";
  const grid    = "var(--plot-grid,  #94a3b8)";
  const fgMuted = "var(--fg-muted,   #64748b)";

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("width", width)
    .attr("height", height)
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height]);

  // Axis
  const y = height/2;
  svg.append("line")
    .attr("x1", pad).attr("x2", width - pad)
    .attr("y1", y).attr("y2", y)
    .attr("stroke", grid).attr("stroke-opacity", 0.6);

  // Arrowheads
  svg.append("path")
    .attr("d", `M ${width-pad} ${y} l -8 -5 l 0 10 z`)
    .attr("fill", grid).attr("fill-opacity", 0.6);

  // Shade Θ0 (left of μ0)
  svg.append("rect")
    .attr("x", pad).attr("y", y - 16)
    .attr("width", mu0x - pad).attr("height", 32)
    .attr("fill", colH0).attr("fill-opacity", 0.22)
    .attr("rx", 6);

  // Shade H1 (right of μ0)
  svg.append("rect")
    .attr("x", mu0x).attr("y", y - 16)
    .attr("width", width - pad - mu0x).attr("height", 32)
    .attr("fill", colH1).attr("fill-opacity", 0.18)
    .attr("rx", 6);

  // μ0 tick
  svg.append("line")
    .attr("x1", mu0x).attr("x2", mu0x)
    .attr("y1", y - 24).attr("y2", y + 24)
    .attr("stroke", grid).attr("stroke-width", 1.1);

  // Labels
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", pad - 8).attr("y", y - 22)
    .text("Parameter space Θ")
    .attr("text-anchor", "start")
    .style("font-size", "12px")
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", mu0x - 6).attr("y", y - 30)
    .text("μ₀")
    .attr("text-anchor", "end")
    .style("font-size", "13px")
    .style("font-weight", 600)
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", (pad + mu0x)/2).attr("y", y + 34)
    .text("Θ₀  (null: μ ≤ μ₀)")
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .style("font-size", "13px")
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", (mu0x + (width - pad))/2).attr("y", y + 34)
    .text("H₁ = Θ \\ Θ₀")
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .style("font-size", "13px")
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  return svg.node();
}
```

### Multidimensional Parameter Space

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-theta-box

thetaBox = {
  const width = 460, height = 200, pad = 20;

  // Big Θ box
  svg.append("rect")
    .attr("x", pad).attr("y", pad)
    .attr("width", width - 2*pad).attr("height", height - 2*pad)
    .attr("rx", 12)
    .attr("fill", "none")
    .attr("stroke", grid).attr("stroke-opacity", 0.6);

  // Label Θ
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", pad + 10).attr("y", pad + 18)
    .text("Θ")
    .style("font-size", "16px")
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  // Θ0 subregion (null) – left rectangle inside Θ
  const innerPad = 14;
  const w0 = (width - 2*pad) * 0.48;
  const h0 = (height - 2*pad) - 2*innerPad;

  svg.append("rect")
    .attr("x", pad + innerPad).attr("y", pad + innerPad)
    .attr("width", w0).attr("height", h0)
    .attr("rx", 10)
    .attr("fill", colH0).attr("fill-opacity", 0.22)
    .attr("stroke", colH0).attr("stroke-opacity", 0.6);

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", pad + innerPad + w0/2).attr("y", pad + innerPad + h0/2)
    .text("Θ₀ (null)")
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .style("font-size", "14px")
    .style("font-weight", 600)
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  // H1 label (complement)
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", pad + innerPad + w0 + 16).attr("y", pad + innerPad + 18)
    .text("H₁ = Θ \\ Θ₀")
    .style("font-size", "14px")
    .style("fill", fgMuted);

  return svg.node();
}
```

:::

We then use the observed data $\underline{x}$ to evaluate whether $H_0$ is plausible. The frequentist reasoning is:

1. **Assume $H_0$ is true.**
2. Use the statistical model to work out what kinds of data would be typical under $H_0$.
3. Compare the actual data with this prediction. If the data look very unusual under $H_0$, this counts against the hypothesis.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
### Terminology: Reject vs. Accept

A hypothesis test produces a **decision rule**, not a logical proof:

- **Reject $H_0$**: the data look very unlikely under $H_0$, so we treat this as evidence against $H_0$.  
- **Fail to reject $H_0$** (sometimes phrased as “accept $H_0$”): the data did not provide strong enough evidence against $H_0$.

Neither outcome proves anything about the *truth* of $H_0$. These terms simply describe which side of the rejection rule the observed data fall on.

In this course we will use **“fail to reject”**, since it emphasises that not rejecting is weaker than proving $H_0$ true. But you should be aware that “accept” is often used informally in practice to mean the same decision.
:::

Suppose our model is

$$
X_i \mid \gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(200, \gamma),
$$

where $\gamma$ is the variance.

We want to test whether $\gamma = 10$. That is:

$$
H_0: \gamma = 10.
$$

The frequentist approach is: *assume $H_0$ is true* and then check whether the observed data are typical of a normal distribution with variance $10$.

```{ojs}
// Parameters
n = 30
mu0 = 200       // null mean
sigma = 10      // std deviation under null
alpha = 0.05

// Slider for observed sample mean
viewof xbar_obs = Inputs.range([mu0 - 3*sigma, mu0 + 3*sigma], 
  {step: 0.5, value: mu0, label: md`Observed sample mean ${tex`\bar{x}_{obs}`}`} )

// Null sampling distribution
xgrid = d3.range(mu0 - 4*sigma, mu0 + 4*sigma, 0.1)
pdf = xgrid.map(x => ({x, y: d3.randomNormal(mu0, sigma/Math.sqrt(n))() })) // or use normal pdf

// Compute rejection region bounds
zcrit = d3.quantile(d3.range(-5,5,0.01), alpha/2) // could just hardcode 1.96
lower = mu0 - 1.96 * sigma/Math.sqrt(n)
upper = mu0 + 1.96 * sigma/Math.sqrt(n)

// Plot
Plot.plot({
  width: 600, height: 300,
  x: {label: "Sample mean"},
  y: {label: "Density"},
  marks: [
    // Null distribution
    Plot.line(xgrid.map(x => ({x, y: 1/(sigma/Math.sqrt(n)*Math.sqrt(2*Math.PI)) 
                                    * Math.exp(-0.5*((x-mu0)/(sigma/Math.sqrt(n)))**2)})), 
              {x:"x", y:"y", stroke: "var(--brand-red)" }),

    // Shaded rejection regions
    Plot.areaY(xgrid.map(x => ({x, y: (x<lower||x>upper) ? 
       1/(sigma/Math.sqrt(n)*Math.sqrt(2*Math.PI)) 
         * Math.exp(-0.5*((x-mu0)/(sigma/Math.sqrt(n)))**2) : 0})), 
       {x:"x", y:"y", fill: "var(--brand-red)", fillOpacity:0.3}),
    
    // Observed value
    Plot.ruleX([xbar_obs], {stroke:"black", strokeWidth:2}),
  ]
})

```

## The Testing Procedure

To make this comparison practical, we do not usually work with the full data distribution. Instead, we reduce the sample to a **test statistic** $T(\underline{X})$ that captures the evidence relevant to $H_0$.

### General Recipe {#sec-general-testing-strategy}

1. **Specify the hypotheses.**  
   Write down the null hypothesis $H_0$ and (optionally) an alternative $H_1$.  
   $H_1$ is not always needed at this stage, but it helps to define what counts as “extreme.”

2. **Choose a test statistic.**  
   Select a statistic $T(\underline{X})$ that would tend to take unusually large or small values if $H_0$ were false.

3. **Find its distribution under $H_0$.**  
   Work out (exactly or approximately) the sampling distribution of $T(\underline{X})$ assuming $H_0$ is true.

4. **Define a rejection region $R_\alpha$.**  
   For a chosen significance level $\alpha$, determine a set $R_\alpha$ of “extreme” values of $T(\underline{X})$ such that  
    $$
    \max_{\theta \in H_0} \, \mathrm{Pr} \big(T \in R_\alpha \mid \theta \big) \;\leq\; \alpha.
    $$

   
   * If $H_0$ is a **single value** (simple null) and $T$ is a **continuous random variable**, this maximum occurs exactly at that value, so we can choose $R_\alpha$ so that the probability equals $\alpha$.
   * If $H_0$ is **composite** or $T$ is **discrete**, the test may be **conservative**: the probability is strictly less than $\alpha$ for some $\theta \in H_0$.

5. **Compute the observed statistic.**  
   From the data, calculate $T_{\text{obs}} = T(\underline{x})$.

6. **Decision.**  
   - If $T_{\text{obs}} \in R_\alpha$, reject $H_0$.  
   - If $T_{\text{obs}} \notin R_\alpha$, fail to reject[^accept-vs-fail-to-reject] $H_0$.


::: {#imp-ing-hypothesis .callout-important collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
### Ingredients of a Hypothesis Test

To define a hypothesis test we need **two choices**:

1. A **test statistic** $T(\underline{X})$ that captures evidence against $H_0$.  
2. A method of constructing the **rejection region** $R_\alpha$ for $T$ at level $\alpha$.

Together, $(T, R_\alpha)$ specify the test completely.

However: 

- There are usually several possible choices of test statistic $T(\underline{X})$.  
  We prefer ones that are **powerful** - i.e. they give a high chance of detecting departures from $H_0$.

- Even once $T$ is chosen, there can be different possible **rejection regions** $R$.  
  By convention we use regions that capture the most extreme values of $T$ in the direction(s) specified by $H_1$.

In addition, the <span class="xref-no-num">[sampling distribution @def-sampling-distribution]</span> the test statistic $T(\underline{X})$ under $H_0$ must be computed. However, it may be obtained *exactly*, or *approximately* by using <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic distributions @imp-term-asymptotic]</span>.

:::

::: {.definition #def-rejection-region}
### Rejection Region

Given a test statistic $T(\underline{X})$ and significance level $\alpha$, a **rejection region** is a subset $R_\alpha$ of the sample space of $T$ such that  

$$
\max_{\theta \in H_0} \, \mathrm{Pr} \big(T \in R_\alpha \mid \theta \big) \;\leq\; \alpha.
$$

This ensures that, no matter which parameter value in $H_0$ is true, the probability of a false rejection (Type I error) never exceeds $\alpha$.

- For a **simple null** with a continuous test statistic, the maximum occurs at the null value itself, and we can usually choose $R_\alpha$ so that the probability equals $\alpha$.  
- For a **composite null** or a **discrete statistic**, the maximum may be strictly less than $\alpha$, making the test *conservative*.  

In practice:  
- For a **two-sided test**, $R_\alpha$ is typically chosen as both tails of the distribution of $T$ under $H_0$.  
- For a **one-sided test**, $R_\alpha$ is typically one tail (upper or lower), depending on the alternative $H_1$.  

Other choices of $R_\alpha$ are mathematically possible, but by convention we use the **most extreme** values of $T$, since this usually maximises power.  
:::

As our first example of a hypothesis test, we will pick a **bad** choice of test statistic $T$ and a couple of choices of rejection region $R$.

::: {#exm-bad-test-statistic}
#### A Terrible Hypothesis Test

Suppose $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ and we wish to test

1. $H_0: \mu = 0$.
2. $H_1: \mu \neq 0$.

We choose $T = X_1$ as our **test statistic**. 

(a) For a chosen $\alpha$, determine *two different* rejection regions.
(b) With the observed sample
  $$
  x_1=0.4,\; x_2=3.2,\; x_3=2.1,\; x_4=2.3,\; x_5=1.8.
  $$
  For which $\alpha$ would you **reject** $H_0$?


```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>
```

**a. Two possible rejection regions**

Under $H_0$, $T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

* **Conventional two-sided test:**
  Reject if $T$ is very large in magnitude:

  $$
  R_\alpha^{(1)} = \{\,|T| > z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\}.
  $$

* **Unconventional one-sided test:**
  Reject if $T$ is very large and positive only:

  $$
  R_\alpha^{(2)} = \{\,T > z_{1-\alpha}\,\}.
  $$

  This region also has probability $\alpha$ under $H_0$, but it only detects positive departures from $0$.

Other choices are mathematically possible (e.g. a left-tail test, or even a symmetric band around $0$ with total mass $\alpha$), but these would be poor at detecting the alternatives we care about.

---

**b. Observed value**

Here $T_{\text{obs}} = x_1 = 0.4$.

* For the two-sided region $R_\alpha^{(1)}$:
  Reject if $|0.4| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$.
  This happens only if $\alpha \gtrsim 0.689$.

* For the one-sided region $R_\alpha^{(2)}$:
  Reject if $0.4 > z_{1-\alpha}$.
  This requires $\alpha \gtrsim 0.345$.

So in both cases you would only reject $H_0$ at extremely large (non-standard) significance levels. At any usual choice like $\alpha=0.05$ or $0.01$, you fail to reject.

---

**Why this test is terrible (and instructive):**

* It **ignores $n-1$ observations**, so the *power* is extremely poor (see @exm-bad-test-statistic-power).
* Different $R_\alpha$ give different answers, showing that both $T$ *and* $R$ matter.
* The statistic $X_1$ is a very unstable indicator of $\mu$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

In @exm-bad-test-statistic we effectively solved for the smallest significance level $\alpha$ at which the observed test statistic would fall in the rejection region.  

This motivates the formal definition of the **$p$-value**:

::: {.definition #def-p-value}
### $p$-value

Given an observed test statistic $T_{\text{obs}}$, the **$p$-value** is the smallest significance level $\alpha$ for which $T_{\text{obs}} \in R_\alpha$.  

Equivalently, it is the probability, under $H_0$, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as $T_{\text{obs}}$:  

$$
p = \Pr \big( T \text{ is at least as extreme as } T_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0 \big).
$$

- For a **two-sided test**, “extreme” means either very large or very small values of $T$.  
- For a **one-sided test**, “extreme” means only one direction, determined by $H_1$.  
:::

Almost all tests in practice are either **one-sided** or **two-sided**. Restricting to these two cases fixes the form of the rejection region:

::: {#def-one-two-sided-tests}

### One-Sided and Two-Sided Tests

* In a **one-sided test**, the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ specifies a direction.

  * Example: $H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0$ vs. $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$.
  * The rejection region is of the form

    $$
    R_\alpha = \{ T \mid T \geq c_\alpha \},
    $$

    i.e. we only reject for *large* values of $T$.
  * Similarly, if $H_1$ is in the other direction, $H_1:\mu < \mu_0$, then

    $$
    R_\alpha = \{ T \mid T \leq c_\alpha \}.
    $$

* In a **two-sided test**, the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ does not specify a direction (e.g. $H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0$).

  * The rejection region is then in both tails:

    $$
    R_\alpha = \{ T \mid |T| \geq c_\alpha \}.
    $$
  * Here, the $\alpha$ level is usually split between the two tails, so each tail has probability $\alpha/2$ under $H_0$.

:::



### Types of Errors

Because decisions are based on data (which vary by chance), mistakes are inevitable.  

A hypothesis test produces a yes/no decision about $H_0$. Comparing this decision with the true state of $H_0$ gives four logical possibilities.

| Decision                    | Reality: $H_0$ true                               | Reality: $H_0$ false                      |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| **Reject $H_0$**         | **Type I Error** (wrongly rejecting a true $H_0$) | Correct decision                             |
| **Fail to reject $H_0$** | Correct decision                                     | **Type II Error** (missing a false $H_0$) |


::: {#def-test-errors}
#### Errors in Hypothesis Tests

- **Type I Error (False Positive):** Rejecting $H_0$ when it is actually true.  
- **Type II Error (False Negative):** Failing to reject $H_0$ when the alternative is true.

By the definition of the <span class="xref-no-num">[rejection region @def-rejection-region]</span>, the probability of a Type I Error is exactly the **significance level** $\alpha$.
:::

### Power of a Test

To describe both types of error within a single framework, we define the **power function**:

::: {#def-power}
#### Power Function

The **power function** of a test is
$$
\beta(\theta) = \Pr\!\big(T \in R_\alpha \mid \theta\big), \qquad \theta \in \Theta.
$$

- If $\theta \in H_0$, this is the **type I error probability**, which by design is at most $\alpha$.  
- If $\theta \in H_1$, this is the probability of **correctly rejecting $H_0$** at that parameter value.

Thus the power function unifies the error probabilities: it is small on $H_0$, and we hope it is large on $H_1$.

:::

- **High power** means the test is good at detecting departures from $H_0$.  
- **High specificity** means the test is good at not raising false alarms.  

In practice, there is a **trade-off**: lowering $\alpha$ reduces false positives but usually reduces power too.

Computing the **power** of a test depends on the true value of the parameter $\theta$:

::: {#exm-bad-test-statistic-power}
#### The Power of a Terrible Hypothesis Test

Continuing from @exm-bad-test-statistic, for each of the *rejection regions*

1. $R_\alpha^{(1)} = \{\,|T| > z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\}$, and

2. $R_\alpha^{(2)} = \{\,T > z_{1-\alpha}\,\},$

derive the **power functions** of the test as a function of $\mu$.


```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>
```

The *alternative* hypothesis is $H_1: \mu \neq 0$. If $H_1$ were true, then our test statistic would have distribution
$$
T = X_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1), \quad \mu \neq 0.
$$

**1. $R_\alpha^{(1)}$**

For $R_\alpha^{(1)}$, we reject if the test statistic $T$ satisfies $|T| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$, we can compute this as:

\begin{align*}
\Pr(|T| > z_{1-\alpha/2}) &= \Pr(T > z_{1-\alpha/2}) + \Pr(T < - z_{1-\alpha/2}) \\
&= \Pr\left( \frac{T - \mu}{1} > z_{1-\alpha/2} \right) + \Pr\left( \frac{T - \mu}{1} < - z_{1-\alpha/2} \right) \\
&= \Pr\left(Z > \mu + z_{1-\alpha/2} \right) + \Pr\left(Z < \mu - z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) \\
&= 1 - \Phi(\mu +  z_{1-\alpha/2}) + \Phi(\mu - z_{1-\alpha/2}),
\end{align*}
where $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $\Phi$ is its CDF.

**2. $R_\alpha^{(2)}$**

For $R_\alpha^{(2)}$, we reject if the test statistic $T$ satisfies $T > z_{1-\alpha}$, we can compute this as:

\begin{align*}
\Pr(T > z_{1-\alpha}) &= \Pr\left(\frac{Z - \mu}{1} > z_{1-\alpha}\right) \\
&= \Pr(Z > z_{1-\alpha} + \mu) \\
&= 1 - \Phi(z_{1-\alpha} + \mu),
\end{align*}
where $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $\Phi$ is its CDF.


---

**Summary**

* For the **two-sided test**

  $$
  \beta(\mu) 
  = \Pr(|T| > z_{1-\alpha/2} \mid \mu) 
  = 1 - \Big[ \Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2} - \mu) - \Phi(-z_{1-\alpha/2} - \mu)\Big].
  $$

  This is one minus the probability that $T$ falls inside the acceptance region.

* For the **one-sided test**

  $$
  \beta(\mu) 
  = \Pr(T > z_{1-\alpha} \mid \mu) 
  = 1 - \Phi(z_{1-\alpha} - \mu).
  $$

Both expressions reduce to $\beta(0) = \alpha$ when $\mu=0$, as required.

```{=html}
</details>
```

```{ojs}
// === Power curves for one- vs two-sided tests ===

// Domain for μ and grid
muDomain = [-4, 4]
muXs = d3.scaleLinear().domain(muDomain).ticks(401)

// Standard normal PDF/CDF helpers
SQRT2 = Math.sqrt(2)
SQRT2PI = Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)

// erf approximation (Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26)
erf = (x) => {
  const sign = Math.sign(x);
  x = Math.abs(x);
  const a1 = 0.254829592, a2 = -0.284496736, a3 = 1.421413741;
  const a4 = -1.453152027, a5 = 1.061405429, p = 0.3275911;
  const t = 1 / (1 + p * x);
  const y = 1 - (((((a5 * t + a4) * t) + a3) * t + a2) * t + a1) * t * Math.exp(-x*x);
  return sign * y;
}

normalCDF = (x) => 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / SQRT2))

// Inverse normal CDF (Acklam's approximation, high accuracy)
function normalInvCDF(p){
  // Coefficients
  const a = [-3.969683028665376e+01,  2.209460984245205e+02, -2.759285104469687e+02,
              1.383577518672690e+02, -3.066479806614716e+01,  2.506628277459239e+00];
  const b = [-5.447609879822406e+01,  1.615858368580409e+02, -1.556989798598866e+02,
              6.680131188771972e+01, -1.328068155288572e+01];
  const c = [-7.784894002430293e-03, -3.223964580411365e-01, -2.400758277161838e+00,
             -2.549732539343734e+00,  4.374664141464968e+00,  2.938163982698783e+00];
  const d = [ 7.784695709041462e-03,  3.224671290700398e-01,  2.445134137142996e+00,
              3.754408661907416e+00];
  // Break-points
  const plow = 0.02425, phigh = 1 - plow;
  let q, r, x;
  if (p < plow){
    q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(p));
    x = (((((c[0]*q + c[1])*q + c[2])*q + c[3])*q + c[4])*q + c[5]) /
        ((((d[0]*q + d[1])*q + d[2])*q + d[3])*q + 1);
  } else if (p > phigh){
    q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - p));
    x = -(((((c[0]*q + c[1])*q + c[2])*q + c[3])*q + c[4])*q + c[5]) /
          ((((d[0]*q + d[1])*q + d[2])*q + d[3])*q + 1);
  } else {
    q = p - 0.5; r = q*q;
    x = (((((a[0]*r + a[1])*r + a[2])*r + a[3])*r + a[4])*r + a[5]) * q /
        (((((b[0]*r + b[1])*r + b[2])*r + b[3])*r + b[4])*r + 1);
  }
  // One step of Halley refinement
  const e = normalCDF(x) - p;
  const u = e * Math.sqrt(2*Math.PI) * Math.exp(x*x/2);
  return x - u / (1 + x*u/2);
}
// Critical values based on current alpha
z_twoSided = normalInvCDF(1 - alphaValue / 2)
z_oneSided = normalInvCDF(1 - alphaValue)

// Power functions using dynamic critical values
powerTwoSided = (mu) => {
  // Power(μ) = P(|T| > z | μ) = Φ(μ - z) + Φ(-μ - z)
  return normalCDF(mu - z_twoSided) + normalCDF(-mu - z_twoSided);
}

powerOneSided = (mu) => {
  // Power(μ) = P(T > z | μ) = 1 - Φ(z - μ)
  return 1 - normalCDF(z_oneSided - mu);
}

// Build curves
twoSided = muXs.map(mu => ({ mu, y: powerTwoSided(mu), which: "Two-sided" }))
oneSided = muXs.map(mu => ({ mu, y: powerOneSided(mu), which: "One-sided" }))

// Mark the μ=0 point (both equal α)
at0 = [
  { mu: 0, y: powerTwoSided(0), which: "Two-sided" },
  { mu: 0, y: powerOneSided(0), which: "One-sided" }
]


// On-curve label anchors (choose different μ to avoid overlap)
muLabelTwo = 2.4
muLabelOne = 1.2
labelDots = [
  { mu: muLabelTwo, y: powerTwoSided(muLabelTwo), label: "Two-sided", color: "var(--brand-teal)" },
  { mu: muLabelOne, y: powerOneSided(muLabelOne), label: "One-sided", color: "var(--brand-red)" }
]


```

```{ojs}
}
```

## Exact Hypothesis Tests

In this section, we derive commonly used hypothesis tests and consider their power.

### One-Sample Normal (known variance)

In @exm-bad-test-statistic, we considered i.i.d. normally distributed data with known variance. However, we considered a **bad** test statistic. For general i.i.d. $X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, it is much more natural to use the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span>,
$$
\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$
to test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs. either a one-sided or two-sided alternative. Let's do this:

::: {#exm-one-sample-normal-known-var-test}
### One-Sample Normal Test (known variance)

Suppose we have i.i.d. data $X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. Suppose we wish to test:

1. $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$, $H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0$.
1. $H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0$, $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$.
2. $H_0: \mu \geq \mu_0$, $H_1: \mu < \mu_0$.

Using the test statistic:
$$
T = \bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,
$$

derive the **one-sided** and **two-sided** rejection regions at significance level $\alpha$.

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>
```

**1.**

Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic $T$ has distribution:
$$
T \mid \mu = \mu_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_0, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$
Since the alternative is two-sided, we want power in both directions and so pick a two-sided rejection region. We have
$$
\frac{T - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
$$
Therefore, since

\begin{align*}
\Pr\left( \frac{T - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \geq z_{1-\alpha/2}  \;\middle|\; \mu = \mu_0 \right) 
+ \Pr\left( \frac{T - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \leq -z_{1-\alpha/2}  \;\middle|\; \mu = \mu_0 \right) 
&= 1-\alpha \\
\Pr\left( \,|T - \mu_0| \geq \frac{z_{1-\alpha/2} \sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\middle|\; \mu = \mu_0 \right) 
&= 1-\alpha.
\end{align*}

Therefore, a valid two-sided $1-\alpha$ rejection region takes the form:
$$
R_\alpha = \left\{ T \mid \; |T - \mu_0| > \frac{\sigma \, z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n}} \right\}.
$$

**2.**

Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic $T$ has distribution:
$$
T \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right), \quad \text{for } \mu \leq \mu_0. 
$$

The null hypothesis does not fully specify the distribution of the null.

[^accept-vs-fail-to-reject]: It is common to say “reject $H_0$” when the $p$-value is small, and “fail to reject $H_0$” otherwise. Both phrases should be interpreted with care: rejecting $H_0$ does **not** prove it is false, and failing to reject $H_0$ does **not** prove it is true. Instead, hypothesis testing provides a decision rule about whether the data are sufficiently inconsistent with $H_0$ at a chosen significance level.
